annotations.text:
1. Home

Four services, not sixteen tiles. These are the four you actually use, and the row reorders itself as that changes. Everything else is behind More.

Under them are the cards written for today, and two of the three are services. The bill you have to pay and the data you are about to run out of come to you, so you never tap through the grid for them at all.

2. Asking

Saying what you want skips the whole form. Buying airtime by hand is five steps: pick the service, pick the network, type the number, type the amount, confirm.

Said out loud it is one sentence, and the app fills the five steps in for you.

3. An answer

The answer is a card, not a paragraph. The chips under the chart are the question itself, so you tap to change it instead of asking again.

At the bottom the app does the arithmetic you would not have done, and offers a plan that costs less than what you are doing now.

4. Sending money

This is the one card the whole app is built on. Everything it prepares looks like this, whether it is a transfer, airtime, a bill or a loan.

Every field it guessed is tinted and says where it came from. Tap any tinted field to correct it. Nothing moves until you slide.

5. Standing instructions

This is where a service stops being a task. The first two rules started life as the offers you saw on the bill screen and the receipt.

One rule per card, each with a switch and a record of what it did. The list underneath says what it will never do on its own.

6. All services

The grid stays, because people learn where things are and tapping is faster than talking when you already know what you want. But only eight tiles get one, and they are the eight you use.

Everything else is grouped rows, which keep working at forty services when a grid has long since stopped. The field at the top is the same input as everywhere else, so searching and asking are one thing.

7. Buying data

The same card as sending money. That is the whole point. Forty services, one thing to learn.

The bundles underneath let you change your mind without saying anything again, and the faces are the people you top up, since most airtime in Nigeria is bought for somebody else.

8. Paying a bill

What comes out of a service matters as much as what goes in. A prepaid meter token is twenty digits you have to type into a box on your wall, so it gets the biggest text on the screen and a copy button.

Then the app offers to do it every month, which is how a one off becomes a standing instruction.

9. Bills

One place for everything that repeats, with what is covered and what is not. The app watches the dates so you do not have to.

The card at the bottom is the same offer again, aimed at the two nobody is watching.

10. A loan

A loan is not a purchase, so it does not get the purchase card. It gets the whole cost on one screen: what you get, what it costs, what you pay back and when.

The app never brings a loan up on its own. It only appears when you ask, and the late fee is on the same screen as the money, not buried in terms you have to open.

11. Virtual card

A card for one thing, with a limit and a switch to freeze it. Naming it after what it is for is what makes it useful.

The line in the middle is the app telling you what the card has actually done, which is the sort of thing you would otherwise have to go and count.

The problem with adding services

Every app in this market ends up with sixteen coloured tiles on the home screen, and it breaks the moment you add the seventeenth.

So the services sit on three surfaces doing three different jobs.

The grid is for finding things. It shows only the handful you use, and the rest are grouped rows behind it.

The sentence is for speed. Saying what you want collapses a five step form into one line, which is where the app earns its keep.

The card is for confirming. Every service, all forty of them, ends in the same card with the same slide. One thing to learn, not forty.

Two type styles, and only two.

Money and interface text are set in Libre Franklin. Anything the app wrote is set in Newsreader, a serif.

So a reader can always tell which part of the screen is a fact from the bank and which part is the app talking.

One accent colour, kept for the app's own voice and for the action it is proposing. Money stays neutral apart from green for money coming in and red for a bill nobody is watching.

Try the other accents on the row of chips above any screen.

On the Naira sign

Google serves these fonts in pieces and none of the pieces contain the Naira sign, so loading them the normal way puts every Naira sign in a different typeface from the digits next to it.

The screens carry their own cut down copies of the fonts instead, so the sign matches. There is also a hair of space after it, or the two bars read as a line through the number.

The name, the account numbers, the meter number and the amounts are all made up. Merchant tiles are grey squares on purpose, since real logos would come from your own data.

Tell me what the real ones should be and I will change them.
